manifest.summaryEvidence: Illustrations by Owen Pomery Imagine a planet that’s home not only to the seven continents you know but also to an immense feature you’ve never heard of, continental in scale. Extending along the world’s coastal shelves from the tropics almost to the poles, this place is roughly equivalent in size to South America, with a total area of more than 6.6 million square miles. During the last Ice Age, it consisted almost entirely of lowland ecosystems: cold grasslands and tundras in the far north, grazed by woolly mammoths and steppe bison; temperate woodlands and open country in the middle latitudes, home to aurochs, horses, and giant elk; tropical forests, grasslands, and mangrove swamps near the equator, inhabited by Stegodons, Asian hippos, and Komodo dragons; and dry scrub in the far south, roamed by marsupial lions, giant flightless birds, and lizards the size of crocodiles. Great rivers, fed by an abundance of lakes and smaller streams, cut their way through many of these lowlands, eventually opening out into marshes, lagoons, estuaries, and tidal flats as they approached the coast. Imagine that human beings settled this place after migrating out of Africa. As they dispersed, they developed technologies and vessels that allowed them to travel by sea; they devised hunting and fishing techniques that allowed them to accumulate surpluses of food and establish small permanent settlements; they buried their dead, built monumental structures, and organized themselves into social hierarchies. On a Hallmark movie set, it is always Christmas but rarely winter. When you produce dozens of original holiday movies a year, there is only so much year for filming, and so you often find yourself making Christmas in July. As I am doing now in Canterbury, England. It doesn’t reliably snow in Canterbury anymore, even in actual winter, but there is snow on the ground. A man from Snowboy Systems, a producer of artificial snow from the East Midlands, is hosing down the sidewalk; the artificial snow on the sidewalk looks less artificial, he says, when the sidewalk is damp. This sidewalk snow is made from biodegradable paper and has the consistency of wet string cheese. Lining the sides of the cathedral are long strips of fleecy, fluffy artificial snow, like the kind in a department-store window. We are setting up for the big final kiss in the snow—a Hallmark Christmas needs a big final kiss in the snow—and that snow, falling from on high, will be made of foam. Three different types of fake snow in a single day of filming! That is what I’m here to study: how to make something so expertly fake that it feels real. manifest.title: Reading Isn’t Over Yet
manifest.summaryEvidence: The Age of Reading Is Over In the August issue, Rose Horowitch considered whether civilization can survive our postliterate era . Rose Horowitch’s “The Age of Reading Is Over” is devastating. The comparison between our present moment and the long, undramatic decline of the Library of Alexandria is apt: We are witnessing a gradual failure of will and attention. I am a conductor, and I was struck by the parallel with musical literacy. A score, like a serious book, demands an ability to hold a complex structure in your mind and resist the urge to skim. When that capacity atrophies, music becomes background, atmosphere, content. The difference between reading Doctor Zhivago and reading a romantasy novel is not unlike the difference between listening to a late Beethoven quartet and letting a playlist wash over you. David Woodard Tampere, Finland While I appreciate Rose Horowitch’s deep dive into the decline of literacy, I take issue with conflating concern about reading in general with concern about the specific kinds of literature people are reading. One series I love, “The Empyrean,” was among those ridiculed in the article. Years ago, I absorbed such judgments subconsciously, and it caused me to take a decade-long break from reading.
